beats.say: 7 x, plus 18, equals 95. Someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then added 18, and got 95. Let's work backwards and find that number.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The plus 18 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 18, we take away 18.

beats.say: And here is the rule of the balance: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So 18 comes off both sides.
On the left, plus 18 and minus 18 cancel each other out. On the right, 95 minus 18 makes 77.
It is tempting to stop here and say 77. But that is 7 x, and we want just x. 7 x means 7 times x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7.
77 divided by 7 is 11. So x equals 11. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 11 back in place of x. 7 times 11 is 77, and 77 plus 18 is 95. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Look at this one. 5 x, minus 3, equals 47. We want x standing all on its own, so we can see what it is worth.
An equation is like a balance: both sides weigh the same, and we must keep it that way. What should we do first?

ask.ifNot: If we divided first, the 3 would have to be divided as well, and that gets messy. It is easier to clear the minus 3 first, by doing the opposite.

beats.say: We add 3 to both sides. Plus is the opposite of minus, so that clears the minus 3 away.
On the left the minus 3 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 47 plus 3 is 50. So 5 x equals 50.
It is tempting to stop here and say 50. But that is 5 x, and we want just x. 5 x means 5 times x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 5.
50 divided by 5 is 10. So x equals 10. There is our hidden number!
Let's test it in the equation we started with. 5 times 10 is 50. Then 50 minus 3 gives 47, just as it should.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!

Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 5 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 5 x has a plus 11 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: The opposite of plus 11 is minus 11. Whatever we do to one side we do to the other, so I write it under both.
On the left, plus 11 and minus 11 cancel each other out. On the right, 26 minus 11 makes 15.
Careful, we are not finished. 15 is what 5 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 5 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 5 x is 5 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 15 into 5 equal parts. That is dividing by 5.

Here is our equation. 3 x, minus 4 times the bracket x plus 6, equals 0. The bracket is the tricky part, so we open it first.
The minus 4 multiplies both things in the bracket. Minus 4 times x is minus 4 x. What is minus 4 times plus 6?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 6 is 24, and the minus sign in front of the 4 comes along too. So it is minus 24. This is the slip to watch for.

beats.say: So the bracket opens into minus 4 x, minus 24.
Now gather the x terms. 3 x take away 4 x: we have 3 and we need to take 4, so we are one x short. That is minus x.
We want a plain x, standing on its own. What could we do to both sides?

ask.ifNot: The x has a minus in front of it. Adding x to both sides undoes that minus x, and puts a plain x on the right.

beats.say: Add x to both sides. On the left, minus x and plus x cancel, leaving minus 24. On the right, 0 plus x is just x.
So x equals minus 24. A negative answer is perfectly fine.
Check it. 3 times minus 24 is minus 72. Inside the bracket, minus 24 plus 6 is minus 18, and minus 4 times minus 18 is plus 72. Minus 72 plus 72 is 0.
The plan: open the bracket, taking the minus sign to every term inside. Then gather the x terms and keep the balance.
We have three expressions, and sum means add them all. So I write them in one long line.
Look for partners that cancel. Which term cancels the very first a?

ask.ifNot: a and minus a are opposites. Put together, they make nothing at all.

beats.say: So a and minus a cancel. I cross them both out.
Now the b terms. There is a b, another b, and a minus 2 b. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: b and b make 2 b. Then minus 2 b takes both of them away again. Nothing is left.

beats.say: One b and another b make 2 b, and then minus 2 b takes them away. So the b terms vanish too.
Only the plain numbers are left: minus 1, plus 1, and plus 1. Minus 1 and plus 1 cancel, so 1 remains.
So the whole sum is just 1. All those letters, and they disappear completely!
Let's test with real numbers. Say a is 2 and b is 3. The three parts become 4, 2 and minus 5. And 4 plus 2 minus 5 is 1.
To add expressions: write them in a line, then gather each family. a with a, b with b, numbers with numbers.
A cafe puzzle. Toast and tea cost 4 rupees. 2 toasts and 2 sandwiches cost 9. A sandwich and 2 teas cost 2. We want the cost of one of each.
Look at the middle line. 2 toasts and 2 sandwiches cost 9 rupees. So what do 1 toast and 1 sandwich cost?

ask.ifNot: Half as much food costs half as much money. Half of 9 rupees is 4 and a half rupees.

beats.say: Half of 9 is 4 and a half. So a toast and a sandwich together cost 4 and a half rupees.
Compare two lines. Toast and tea cost 4. Toast and sandwich cost 4 and a half. The toast is the same in both. So which costs more, the sandwich or the tea?

choices: the sandwich, by half a rupee
the tea, by half a rupee
ask.ifNot: Only one thing changed: the tea became a sandwich. And the price went up by half a rupee. So the sandwich costs half a rupee more than the tea.

beats.say: 4 and a half, minus 4, is a half. So a sandwich is a tea plus half a rupee.
Now use the last line: a sandwich and 2 teas cost 2 rupees. Swap the sandwich for a tea plus a half. That gives 3 teas, plus a half, making 2.
Take the half away from both sides, and 3 teas cost 1 and a half rupees. Share that by 3, and one tea costs half a rupee.
A sandwich is half a rupee more than that, so 1 rupee. And toast plus tea is 4, so the toast is 4 minus a half, which is 3 and a half.
Now add one of each: 3 and a half, plus 1, plus a half. That is 5 rupees.
Check the middle line. 2 toasts are 7 rupees and 2 sandwiches are 2 rupees. 7 plus 2 is 9. It fits.
So with a puzzle like this: compare two lines that share something, see what changed, and work out one price at a time.
Five gifts, costing 21 rupees in all. And we know four pair totals. We want A and E together.
Look at two of the pairs: A with B, and C with D. Together they cover four gifts. Which gift is left out?

ask.ifNot: A, B, C and D are all inside those two pairs. The only gift not counted is E.

beats.say: So take those two pairs away from the total, and what is left is E. 21 minus 6 minus 7 is 8.
Now we want A. Which two pairs leave only A out?

ask.ifNot: We need two pairs that cover B, C, D and E, with no A in them. That is B with C, together with D and E.

beats.say: B and C cost 10, and D and E cost 9. 21 minus 10 minus 9 is 2. So A costs 2 rupees.
A is 2 and E is 8. Together, 2 plus 8 is 10 rupees.
Let's check with the others. B is 6 minus 2, which is 4. C is 10 minus 4, which is 6. D is 7 minus 6, which is 1. And D plus E is 1 plus 8, which is 9. It all fits.
When you know a total and some pairs, take away pairs that do not overlap. Whatever is left out is what you have found.
Five people, and their ages add up to 105. We know four pair totals. We need the youngest, so we have to find everyone.
A and B make 39, and C and D make 38. Those two pairs cover four people. Who is left out?

ask.ifNot: A, B, C and D are all inside those two pairs. The only person not counted is E.

beats.say: So E is the total, minus those two pairs. 105 minus 39 minus 38 is 28.
The same trick finds A. B and C make 40, D and E make 44, and only A is left out. 105 minus 40 minus 44 is 21.
Now we know A is 21. Which fact gives us B straight away?

ask.ifNot: We want a fact with B and one other person whose age we already know. A and B make 39, and we know A.

beats.say: B is 39 minus 21, which is 18. Then C is 40 minus 18, which is 22. And D is 38 minus 22, which is 16.
Line them up: A is 21, B is 18, C is 22, D is 16 and E is 28. The smallest is 16.
Check the one pair we did not use. D and E are 16 plus 28, which is 44. Just what the question said.
So with a total and some pairs: remove pairs that do not overlap to find one person, then walk along the chain. The youngest is 16.
Four children, and their ages add up to 20. We want Anil's age, so let's call Anil's age a.
Anil is 3 years younger than Chetan. So how do we write Chetan's age?

ask.ifNot: If Anil is 3 years younger, then Chetan is 3 years older than Anil. Older means we add: a plus 3.

beats.say: So Chetan is a plus 3. David is 5 years older than Chetan, so David is a plus 3 plus 5, which is a plus 8.
David is 3 years older than Bunty, so Bunty is 3 years younger than David. That makes Bunty a plus 8 minus 3, which is a plus 5.
Now add all four ages, and that must be 20.
Gather the like terms. There are 4 lots of a. And the plain numbers, 5 and 3 and 8, make 16.
Now it is an equation we know. What do we do first?

ask.ifNot: The 4 a has a plus 16 hanging on to it. We clear that first, by taking 16 from both sides.

beats.say: Take 16 from both sides. 20 minus 16 is 4, so 4 a equals 4.
Divide both sides by 4. 4 divided by 4 is 1. So Anil is just 1 year old.
Check the story. Anil is 1, so Chetan is 4, David is 9 and Bunty is 6. 1 plus 6 plus 4 plus 9 is 20. It fits.
So in a word problem: give a letter to the thing you want, write everyone else using that letter, and build one equation.
Two lines here. The first is a fact: 2 x, plus 1, equals 8. The second is what we must find: 4 x, plus 1.
Start with the fact. How do we get the 2 x on its own?

ask.ifNot: The 2 x has a plus 1 with it. To undo plus 1 we do the opposite, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: To undo plus 1 we take away 1, on both sides. 8 minus 1 is 7. So 2 x equals 7.
We could divide by 2 now to find x. But look at what we need: 4 x. How is 4 x related to 2 x?

ask.ifNot: 4 is 2 times 2. So 4 x is 2 lots of 2 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 4 x is double 7, which is 14.
Do not stop there! The question wants 4 x, plus 1. 14 plus 1 is 15.
We can check by finding x after all. 2 x is 7, so x is 7 divided by 2, which is 3.5. And 4 times 3.5, plus 1, gives 15 again.
The plan: find 2 x first, scale it up to 4 x, then finish with the plus 1. No need for x on its own.
We are dividing 12 x y plus 8 y by 4 y. Quotient is just the name for the answer to a division.
There are two parts being divided. What does the 4 y divide?

choices: each part, one at a time
ask.ifNot: When a sum is divided, every part of the sum is divided. Like sharing 2 bags of sweets: you share out each bag.

beats.say: So we split it into two little divisions. 12 x y divided by 4 y, and 8 y divided by 4 y.
Take the first one. Numbers first: 12 divided by 4 is 3. Then the letters: there is a y on top and a y underneath.
What is y divided by y?

ask.ifNot: Any number divided by itself is 1. 7 divided by 7 is 1, and y divided by y is 1 too. So the y simply cancels.

beats.say: So the y cancels, and the x is left. 12 x y divided by 4 y is 3 x.
Now the second part. 8 divided by 4 is 2, and the y cancels again. So we just get 2.
Put the two answers together: 3 x plus 2.
Check by multiplying back. 4 y times 3 x is 12 x y, and 4 y times 2 is 8 y. That is exactly what we started with.
To divide a sum: divide each part, numbers by numbers, and cancel any letter that is on both the top and the bottom.
This question does not want the two numbers. It wants the equation: the sentence, written in maths, using m.
Consecutive means next to each other. Here are some odd numbers in a row: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. How far apart are neighbours?

ask.ifNot: From 3 to 5 we jump over the 4. So odd numbers that are neighbours are always 2 apart.

beats.say: So if the first odd number is m, the next one is m plus 2.
The question says the sum of the two numbers is 12. What does the word sum tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: Sum is the answer to an addition. So we add the first number and the next number.

beats.say: So we add them, and that must equal 12. m, plus m plus 2, equals 12.
Look at the other choices. m times m plus 2 would be the product, not the sum. m plus 2 equals 12 uses only the second number. And 2 m would mean both numbers are the same.
Does our equation make sense? 5 and 7 are both odd, and they are neighbours. And 5 plus 7 is 12. It fits.
To turn words into an equation: name the first number, write the others from it, then follow the key word. Sum means add.
Here is our equation. 4 a, minus 5, equals 2 a, plus 3. This time the letter is on both sides.
We want all the a terms on one side. Which move does that?

ask.ifNot: The 2 a on the right is a plus 2 a. To undo it we take 2 a away, and we take it from both sides so the balance stays level.

beats.say: So we take 2 a from both sides. On the right it is gone. On the left, 4 a take away 2 a leaves 2 a.
Now it is one we know well. What is in the way of the 2 a?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 2 a has a minus 5 hanging on to it. That goes next.

beats.say: To undo minus 5 we add 5, to both sides. 3 plus 5 is 8, so 2 a equals 8.
2 a means 2 times a, so we divide both sides by 2. 8 divided by 2 is 4. So a equals 4.
Check both sides with a as 4. Left: 4 times 4, minus 5, is 11. Right: 2 times 4, plus 3, is 11. Both sides are 11, so it balances.
When the letter is on both sides: gather the letters on one side, then the numbers on the other, then divide.
Something divides 91 a b c and gives 7 c. We have to find that something.
Try the idea with small numbers. 12 divided by 4 is 3. And if we did not know the 4, we could find it: 12 divided by 3 is 4.
So to find a missing divider, we divide the big one by the answer. Our missing piece is 91 a b c divided by 7 c.
Numbers first. What is 91 divided by 7?

ask.ifNot: Try 7 times 13. 7 times 10, and 7 times 3, added together make 91. So 91 divided by 7 is 13.

beats.say: 91 divided by 7 is 13.
Now the letters: a b c divided by c. What is left?

ask.ifNot: There is a c on top and a c underneath. c divided by c is 1, so the c cancels. Only a b is left.

beats.say: The c on top and the c below cancel each other, leaving a b.
Put the number and the letters together: 13 a b.
Check by multiplying back. 13 times 7 is 91, and a b times c is a b c. So 13 a b times 7 c really is 91 a b c.
So to find a missing divider, divide by the answer instead. Numbers with numbers, and cancel matching letters.
We are told that 2 x, minus 3, equals 10. And we are asked for 4 x, minus 5. Notice the question never asks for x itself.
Start with the fact. How do we get the 2 x on its own?

ask.ifNot: The 2 x has a minus 3 with it. To undo minus 3 we do the opposite, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: To undo minus 3 we add 3, on both sides. 10 plus 3 is 13. So 2 x equals 13.
We could divide by 2 now to find x. But look at what we need: 4 x. How is 4 x related to 2 x?

ask.ifNot: 4 is 2 times 2. So 4 x is 2 lots of 2 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 4 x is double 13, which is 26.
Do not stop there! The question wants 4 x, minus 5. 26 minus 5 is 21.
We can check by finding x after all. 2 x is 13, so x is 13 divided by 2, which is 6.5. And 4 times 6.5, minus 5, gives 21 again.
The plan: find 2 x first, scale it up to 4 x, then finish with the minus 5. No need for x on its own.
We know a is 3 and b is 5, and c is made from them. Then we compare three expressions, to see which is greatest.
c first. c is b minus a, so 5 minus 3, which is 2.
Take the first expression: a plus c, in a bracket, times b. With the numbers in, that is 3 plus 2, times 5. What do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Brackets always come first. So we add 3 and 2 before we multiply.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5, and 5 times 5 is 25.
The second one: a plus b, times c. 3 plus 5 is 8, and 8 times 2 is 16.
The third: b plus c, times a. 5 plus 2 is 7, and 7 times 3 is 21.
So the three values are 25, 16 and 21. The greatest is 25, and that came from a plus c, times b.
Notice they are not all equal, even though the same three numbers are used each time. So: find every letter, put the numbers in, do the brackets first, then compare.
Here we are not solving anything. We are translating a sentence into an equation, with m standing for a number.
Consecutive means next to each other. Here are some odd numbers in a row: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. How far apart are neighbours?

ask.ifNot: From 3 to 5 we jump over the 4. So odd numbers that are neighbours are always 2 apart.

beats.say: So if the first odd number is m, the next one is m plus 2.
The question says the sum of the two numbers is 16. What does the word sum tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: Sum is the answer to an addition. So we add the first number and the next number.

beats.say: So we add them, and that must equal 16. m, plus m plus 2, equals 16.
The other choices each miss something. m plus 2 equals 16 forgets the first number. 2 m treats the two numbers as equal. And m times m plus 2 multiplies, when sum means add.
Does our equation make sense? 7 and 9 are both odd, and they are neighbours. And 7 plus 9 is 16. It fits.
So the plan: give the first number a letter, build the second from it, and let the word sum tell you to add.
Here is an equation with fractions. m plus 6, all over 11, equals m over 9. Fractions are awkward, so first we get rid of them.
Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. If we multiply both sides by 11 and by 9, both bottoms disappear. People call this cross multiplying.
Now open the bracket. What does the 9 multiply?

ask.ifNot: The 9 is outside the bracket, so it multiplies everything inside: the m, and the 6 as well.

beats.say: 9 times m is 9 m, and 9 times 6 is 54.
m is on both sides. Take the smaller lot, 9 m, away from both sides. On the right, 11 m take away 9 m leaves 2 m.
54 equals 2 m. How do we find one m?

ask.ifNot: 2 m means 2 times m. Divide undoes times, so we halve both sides.

beats.say: Half of 54 is 27. So m equals 27.
Put 27 back. On the left, 27 plus 6 is 33, and 33 over 11 is 3. On the right, 27 over 9 is 3. Both sides are 3.
With a fraction on each side, cross multiply to clear the bottoms. After that it is an ordinary equation.
Two friends are sending messages. Arnav sends m messages every hour, for 5 hours. Pranav sends p every hour, for 4 hours. We want the total.

board.text: Arnav: m each hour, for 5 hours
Pranav: p each hour, for 4 hours

beats.say: Imagine m was 3. Then Arnav sends 3, and 3, and 3, and 3, and 3. That is 5 lots of 3.
So with m messages each hour, for 5 hours, how many does Arnav send?

ask.ifNot: m each hour for 5 hours is m, 5 times over. And 5 lots of m is written 5 m.

beats.say: 5 lots of m. We write that as 5 m.
Pranav is the same idea. p messages each hour for 4 hours is 4 lots of p, which is 4 p.
Total means add. Can we join 5 m and 4 p into one term, like 9 m p?

choices: No: m and p are different letters
ask.ifNot: m and p stand for different numbers, so they are not like terms. We can only write them side by side, with a plus between.

beats.say: So the total is 5 m plus 4 p.
Test it. Say m is 2 and p is 3. Arnav sends 10, Pranav sends 12, and that is 22 altogether. And 5 times 2, plus 4 times 3, is 22.
So so many each hour, for so many hours, means multiply. And different letters always stay apart.
Here is our equation. 3 x, plus 7, equals 1, minus 2 x. There is an x on each side, so let's bring them together.
On the right there is a minus 2 x. How do we move it over to the left side?

ask.ifNot: To undo minus 2 x, we add 2 x. And we add it to both sides, so the balance stays level.

beats.say: Add 2 x to both sides. On the right it cancels, leaving 1. On the left, 3 x plus 2 x makes 5 x.
Now undo the plus 7, by taking 7 from both sides.
1 minus 7. We have 1, and we take away 7. Where do we land?

ask.ifNot: Taking 7 from 1 takes us below zero. From 1 down to 0 is 1 step, then 6 more steps down. That lands on minus 6.

beats.say: So 5 x equals minus 6. The last move is the usual one: divide both sides by 5.
Minus 6 divided by 5 does not come out as a whole number, so we leave it as a fraction. x equals minus 6 over 5.
Check with the tidy line, 5 x plus 7 equals 1. 5 times minus 6 over 5 is minus 6. And minus 6 plus 7 is 1. It works.
The plan: letters to one side, numbers to the other, each time by doing the opposite to both sides. And an answer can be a negative fraction.
A fruit seller has apples, mangoes and oranges. We know three pair totals. First we find how many of each he has. Then he sells 100 of each.
Suppose we add all three totals together. How many times does each fruit get counted?

ask.ifNot: Look for A in the three lines: it appears in 2 of them. The same is true for M and for O. So every fruit is counted twice.

beats.say: The three totals add up to 1140. That counts every fruit twice, so we halve it. All the fruit together is 570.
All three make 570, and apples with mangoes make 400. Which fruit does that give us?

ask.ifNot: Take the apples and mangoes away from all the fruit, and only the oranges are left.

beats.say: So oranges are 570 minus 400, which is 170. In the same way, apples are 570 minus 300, which is 270. And mangoes are 570 minus 440, which is 130.
Do not stop here! He sells 100 of each. Apples go down to 170, mangoes to 30, and oranges to 70.
So he has 170 apples, 30 mangoes and 70 oranges left.
Check the starting numbers. 270 apples and 130 mangoes make 400. 130 mangoes and 170 oranges make 300. Both match the question.
So when every pair total is given: add them all, halve, then subtract each pair. And finish the story: 170, 30 and 70.
We are not told a or b. We only know that a divided by b is 2. Yet that is enough to find 4 b over a.
a divided by b is 2. What does that tell us about a and b?

ask.ifNot: 10 divided by 5 is 2, because 10 is 2 times 5. In the same way, a divided by b is 2 means a is 2 times b.

beats.say: So a is double b. Let's pick an easy pair that fits: b is 1 and a is 2.
Now work out 4 b over a. 4 times 1 is 4, and 4 divided by 2 is 2.
Was that luck? Try another pair: b is 3 and a is 6. 4 times 3 is 12, and 12 divided by 6 is 2 again.
Here is why it always works. If a over b is 2, what is b over a, the fraction flipped?

ask.ifNot: Flipping a fraction turns it upside down. 2 is 2 over 1, so upside down it is 1 over 2, a half.

beats.say: b over a is a half. And 4 b over a is 4 times that. 4 times a half is 2.
So when you only know how two letters compare, try easy numbers that fit, then look for the reason. The answer is 2.
Here is what we know: 2 x, plus 1, equals 8. Here is what we want: 4 x, plus 1. Let's see how to get from one to the other.
Start with the fact. What is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 2 x has a plus 1 hanging on to it. We clear that first.

beats.say: To undo plus 1 we take away 1, on both sides. 8 minus 1 is 7. So 2 x equals 7.
We could divide by 2 now to find x. But look at what we need: 4 x. How is 4 x related to 2 x?

ask.ifNot: 4 is 2 times 2. So 4 x is 2 lots of 2 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 4 x is double 7, which is 14.
Do not stop there! The question wants 4 x, plus 1. 14 plus 1 is 15.
We can check by finding x after all. 2 x is 7, so x is 7 divided by 2, which is 3.5. And 4 times 3.5, plus 1, gives 15 again.
So before you solve for the letter, look at what is asked. Sometimes you can build it straight from what you already know.
x is 3 and y is minus 2. We need x y, over x minus y. The negative number makes this one a little tricky, so we go slowly.
Do the top first. x y means x times y, so that is 3 times minus 2. What is 3 times minus 2?

ask.ifNot: 3 lots of minus 2 is minus 2, minus 2, minus 2. That is minus 6. A positive times a negative is negative.

beats.say: So the top is minus 6.
Now the bottom: x minus y. That is 3, minus, minus 2. What does that come to?

ask.ifNot: Taking away a negative is the same as adding. So 3 minus minus 2 is 3 plus 2, which is 5. Writing 3 minus 2 here is the classic slip.

beats.say: Taking away minus 2 is the same as adding 2. So the bottom is 3 plus 2, which is 5.
Top over bottom: minus 6 over 5. It does not divide exactly, so we leave it as a fraction.
A quick sense check. The top is negative and the bottom is positive, so the answer should be negative. And it is: minus 6 over 5.
So: put the numbers in, with brackets round any negative. Work out the top and the bottom separately, then divide.
This question is a sentence we have to turn into maths. A number, increased by 17, equals 60 times the reciprocal of the number.
First, that long word. What is the reciprocal of 5?

ask.ifNot: The reciprocal of a number is 1 divided by that number. It is the number turned upside down. So the reciprocal of 5 is 1 over 5.

beats.say: So 60 times the reciprocal of a number is 60 times 1 over the number. That is just 60 divided by the number. If we call the number n, we get this.
We could solve it, but with four choices it is quicker to test them. Start with 5. 5 plus 17 is 22. But 60 divided by 5 is 12. Not a match.
Now try 3. 3 plus 17 is 20. What is 60 divided by 3?

ask.ifNot: 6 divided by 3 is 2, so 60 divided by 3 is 20.

beats.say: 60 divided by 3 is 20 as well. The two sides match!
And the bigger choices, 17 and 12? Adding 17 makes them bigger still, but 60 divided by a big number is small. So they cannot match.
So the number is 3. When a question gives choices, testing each one in the sentence is a fine way to solve it.
This equation has a bracket on each side. We open the brackets first, and then we solve.
Left side first. The 4 multiplies both things inside. 4 times 2 x is 8 x. And careful: 4 times minus 1 is minus 4.
Now the right side. What does 5 times the bracket, x plus 2, open into?

ask.ifNot: The 5 multiplies the x and the 2. 5 times x is 5 x, and 5 times 2 is 10. So we get 5 x plus 10.

beats.say: So the bracket becomes 5 x plus 10, and the plus 4 is still waiting at the end.
10 and 4 are both plain numbers. Together they make 14.
x is on both sides now. What is a good next move?

ask.ifNot: We want the x terms together. The 5 x on the right is a plus 5 x, so we take 5 x away, from both sides.

beats.say: Take 5 x from both sides. On the right it is gone. On the left, 8 x take away 5 x leaves 3 x.
Undo the minus 4 by adding 4 to both sides. 14 plus 4 is 18, so 3 x equals 18.
Divide both sides by 3. 18 divided by 3 is 6. So x equals 6.
Check. Left: the bracket is 2 times 6, minus 1, which is 11. And 4 times 11 is 44. Right: the bracket is 8, and 5 times 8, plus 4, is also 44.
The plan: open every bracket, tidy each side, bring the letters together, clear the plain number, and divide last.
We are told Z is 7. One of these equations may be true for that Z. An equation is true when both of its sides come out the same.
So how do we test each one?

choices: put 7 in on one side only
put 7 in for Z on both sides
ask.ifNot: We put 7 in place of every Z, on the left and on the right, and then see whether the two sides match.

beats.say: A first. The left side is 5, plus 2 times 7, which is 19. The right side is 3 times 7, plus 2, which is 23. Not the same, so A is out.
Now B. The left side is 5 times 7, plus 6, which is 41. What is the right side, 7 Z minus 8?

ask.ifNot: 7 Z is 7 times 7, which is 49. Take away 8 and we get 41.

beats.say: 7 times 7 is 49, and 49 minus 8 is 41. Both sides are 41. B is true!
Let's be sure about C. The left side is 35 and the right side is 42. Not equal.
So the true equation is 5 Z plus 6 equals 7 Z minus 8.
To test an equation, put the number in on both sides and compare. Equal sides mean it is true.
The word solve here really means simplify. Three brackets are added together, and there are three families of letters: w, s and r.
Let's start with the w family. Which terms go with 4 w?

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter. So 4 w goes with the other w terms: 2 w, and minus 3 w.

beats.say: 4 w plus 2 w is 6 w, and minus 3 w leaves 3 w.
Now the s family. 5 s minus 3 s is 2 s, and 4 s more makes 6 s.
Now the r family: minus 3 r, plus 2 r, plus 4 r. Careful with that first sign. How many r is that?

ask.ifNot: The first one is minus 3 r, so we start 3 below zero. Plus 2 brings us to minus 1, and plus 4 brings us up to 3. So 3 r.

beats.say: Minus 3, plus 2, plus 4 comes to 3. So that is 3 r.
Put the three families side by side: 6 s plus 3 w plus 3 r. The order does not matter, as long as each sign stays with its own term.
Test it with every letter as 1. The three brackets give 6, 1 and 5, which add up to 12. And 6 plus 3 plus 3 is 12 as well.
So to add long expressions: take one letter family at a time, and keep the sign in front of each term.
The job here is to write the sentence as an equation. We do not have to solve it, only to build it, using W.
Consecutive means next to each other. Here are some odd numbers in a row: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. How far apart are neighbours?

ask.ifNot: From 3 to 5 we jump over the 4. So odd numbers that are neighbours are always 2 apart.

beats.say: So if the first odd number is W, the next one is W plus 2.
The question says the sum of the two numbers is 192. What does the word sum tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: Sum is the answer to an addition. So we add the first number and the next number.

beats.say: So we add them, and that must equal 192. W, plus W plus 2, equals 192.
Why not the others? W plus 2 equals 192 leaves out the first number. 2 W would mean two equal numbers. And W squared multiplies, when the word sum tells us to add.
Does our equation make sense? 95 and 97 are both odd, and they are neighbours. And 95 plus 97 is 192. It fits.
To turn words into an equation: name the first number, write the others from it, then follow the key word. Sum means add.
Two jobs in this one. First we solve the equation to find p. Then we use p to work out p plus 3, times p plus 2.
p is on both sides. Which lot of p shall we take away from both sides?

ask.ifNot: Taking away the smaller lot, 2 p, keeps everything positive, and that is much easier to work with.

beats.say: Take 2 p from both sides. On the left only 5 is left. On the right, 9 p take away 2 p is 7 p.
Now undo the minus 30, by adding 30 to both sides. 5 plus 30 is 35.
7 p means 7 times p. Divide both sides by 7, and 35 divided by 7 is 5. So p equals 5.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: Look back at the question. It does not ask for p. It asks for the value of p plus 3, times p plus 2.

beats.say: Put 5 in for p. 5 plus 3 is 8, and 5 plus 2 is 7. 8 times 7 is 56.
Now look at the choices: 84, 14 and 36. Our 56 is not there. So the answer is none of these.
When your answer is not listed, check before you trust it. With p as 5, the left side is 2 times 5, plus 5, which is 15. The right is 9 times 5, minus 30, also 15.
So: solve for the letter, then answer what was really asked. And if your checked answer is not among the choices, none of these is the one to pick.
Two lines here. The first is a fact: 4 x, minus 7, equals 12. The second is what we must find: 12 x, minus 14.
Start with the fact. What is in the way of the 4 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 4 x has a minus 7 hanging on to it. We clear that first.

beats.say: To undo minus 7 we add 7, on both sides. 12 plus 7 is 19. So 4 x equals 19.
We could divide by 4 now to find x. But look at what we need: 12 x. How is 12 x related to 4 x?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 3 times 4. So 12 x is 3 lots of 4 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 12 x is 3 times 19, which is 57.
Do not stop there! The question wants 12 x, minus 14. 57 minus 14 is 43.
We can check by finding x after all. 4 x is 19, so x is 19 divided by 4, which is 4.75. And 12 times 4.75, minus 14, gives 43 again.
So before you solve for the letter, look at what is asked. Sometimes you can build it straight from what you already know.
Only a is given. m is built from a, and p is built from m. So we find them in order, and then compare three expressions.
Which letter can we find first?

ask.ifNot: p needs m, and m needs a. We know a, so m comes first.

beats.say: m is 7 minus 2, which is 5. Then p is 5 plus 5, which is 10.
First expression: m plus p is 15, and 15 times 7 is 105.
Second: p plus a is 17, and 17 times 5 is 85.
Third: a plus m is 12, and 12 times 10 is 120.
We have 105, 85 and 120. Careful now: what does the question want?

ask.ifNot: Read the question again. It asks which one has the least value, so we want the smallest.

beats.say: The smallest is 85, and that came from p plus a, times m.
So: find the letters in order, work out each expression with the bracket first, and check whether the question wants the greatest or the least.
d is 6. We must find which statement is true. True means the left side and the right side are worth the same.
Put 6 in place of d on both sides. For A, the left is 5 times 6, plus 19, which is 49. The right is 7 times 6, minus 17, which is 25. Nowhere near.
Now B. The left side is 8, plus 4 times 6, which is 32. What is the right side, 6 d minus 6?

ask.ifNot: 6 d means 6 times 6. Take 6 away from that, and we get 30.

beats.say: The right side is 30, but the left side was 32. Close, but not equal. B is out.
Now C. The left is 12 times 6, minus 14, which is 58. The right is 16, plus 7 times 6, which is also 58. They match!
So the true statement is 12 d minus 14 equals 16 plus 7 d.
One of them worked, so we do not need none of these. But we only knew that because we tested every one.
To check whether a statement is true: put the number in on both sides, work each side out, and compare.
Here is our equation. 6 x minus 9, equals 4 x plus 30, all over 2. Let's tidy the right side first.
All over 2 means the whole bracket is halved. What is half of 4 x plus 30?

ask.ifNot: The 2 divides both parts. Half of 4 x is 2 x, and half of 30 is 15. Halving only one of them is the slip to avoid.

beats.say: So half of 4 x is 2 x, and half of 30 is 15.
x is on both sides. Take the smaller lot, 2 x, from both sides. 6 x take away 2 x leaves 4 x.
What is in the way of the 4 x now?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 4 x has a minus 9 hanging on to it. That is what we clear next.

beats.say: To undo minus 9 we add 9 to both sides. 15 plus 9 is 24. So 4 x equals 24.
Divide both sides by 4. 24 divided by 4 is 6. So x equals 6.
Check. Left: 6 times 6 is 36, and 36 minus 9 is 27. Right: 4 times 6, plus 30, is 54, and half of 54 is 27. Both sides are 27.
So: tidy any fraction first, bring the x terms together, clear the plain number, then divide.
A fraction on each side this time. 4 x minus 5, over 5, equals 2 x plus 3, over 3. First we clear the bottoms.
Multiply both sides by 5 and by 3. On the left the 5 cancels and the 3 stays. On the right the 3 cancels and the 5 stays. That is cross multiplying.
Open the left bracket. The 3 multiplies the 4 x, and it multiplies the minus 5. What is 3 times minus 5?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 5 is 15, and the minus sign stays with it. So we get minus 15.

beats.say: So the left side is 12 x minus 15. On the right, 5 times 2 x is 10 x, and 5 times 3 is 15.
Take the smaller lot of x, 10 x, from both sides. 12 x take away 10 x leaves 2 x.
What clears the minus 15?

ask.ifNot: Adding undoes taking away. So we add 15, and we add it to both sides.

beats.say: Add 15 to both sides. 15 plus 15 is 30, so 2 x equals 30.
Divide both sides by 2. Half of 30 is 15. So x equals 15.
Check with 15. Left: 4 times 15, minus 5, is 55, and 55 over 5 is 11. Right: 2 times 15, plus 3, is 33, and 33 over 3 is 11. Both sides are 11.
With a fraction on each side: cross multiply, open the brackets, then solve it like any other equation.
Two numbers. Add them and we get 92. Subtract them and we get 14. We want the square of the greater one.
Here is a neat trick: add the two lines together. What happens to the smaller number?

ask.ifNot: In the first line the smaller number is added. In the second it is taken away. Plus smaller and minus smaller cancel each other.

beats.say: So adding the lines leaves 2 lots of the greater number. And that equals 92 plus 14, which is 106.
Half of 106 is 53. So the greater number is 53.
Quick check. The smaller one is 92 minus 53, which is 39. And 53 minus 39 is 14. Good.
Is 53 our answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the square of the greater number. Square means the number times itself.

beats.say: 53 times 53. Split it into two easier parts: 53 times 50 is 2650, and 53 times 3 is 159.
Add them: 2650 plus 159 is 2809. So 53 squared is 2809.
When you know a sum and a difference: add them and halve to get the greater number. Then do exactly what the question asks.
p is 7, and q is built from p. Then there are four expressions, and we want the one with the greatest value.
First q. It is 2 p minus 9. What is 2 p when p is 7?

ask.ifNot: A number next to a letter means times. 2 p is 2 times 7, which is 14.

beats.say: So q is 14 minus 9, which is 5.
Now the first expression. 2 p is 14 and 3 q is 15. 14 minus 15 dips 1 below zero, and plus 5 brings us up to 4.
The second. 4 q is 20 and 2 p is 14. 20 minus 14 is 6.
The third. 7 plus 5 is 12, and 12 minus 12 is 0.
The last one. 7 q is 35, and 5 p is also 35. They cancel each other, and 3 is left.
The four values are 4, 6, 0 and 3. Which expression wins?

ask.ifNot: The greatest of 4, 6, 0 and 3 is 6. And 6 came from 4 q minus 2 p.

beats.say: So 4 q minus 2 p has the greatest value, 6.
Find the missing letter first, work out each expression carefully, and only then compare.
Here is what we know: 4 x, plus 3, equals 22. Here is what we want: 12 x, plus 3. Let's see how to get from one to the other.
Start with the fact. How do we get the 4 x on its own?

ask.ifNot: The 4 x has a plus 3 with it. To undo plus 3 we do the opposite, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: To undo plus 3 we take away 3, on both sides. 22 minus 3 is 19. So 4 x equals 19.
We could divide by 4 now to find x. But look at what we need: 12 x. How is 12 x related to 4 x?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 3 times 4. So 12 x is 3 lots of 4 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 12 x is 3 times 19, which is 57.
Do not stop there! The question wants 12 x, plus 3. 57 plus 3 is 60.
We can check by finding x after all. 4 x is 19, so x is 19 divided by 4, which is 4.75. And 12 times 4.75, plus 3, gives 60 again.
The plan: find 4 x first, scale it up to 12 x, then finish with the plus 3. No need for x on its own.
Three letters, but only a is given. b is built from a, and c is built from b. So we find them in that order.
b first. a minus 1 is 17 minus 1, which is 16. Half of 16 is 8. So b is 8.
Then c is b plus 3. 8 plus 3 is 11.
Now the squares. What does a squared mean, when a is 17?

ask.ifNot: Squared means the number times itself. So 17 squared is 17 times 17, not 17 times 2.

beats.say: 17 times 17 is 289. 11 times 11 is 121. And 8 times 8 is 64.
So we have 289, minus 121, plus 64. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are done from left to right. Adding 121 and 64 first would take away too much.

beats.say: 289 minus 121 is 168. Then 168 plus 64 is 232.
So: find the letters in order, square each one, then work from left to right. The answer is 232.
Here is a five digit number with two stars in it. Both stars hide the same digit, and we are going to find it.
First, look at where the stars sit. Which two places are they in?

ask.ifNot: Count the places from the right. The 9 is in the ones, the 1 is in the tens. Then come the two stars, in the hundreds and the thousands.

beats.say: Let's call the hidden digit d. In the thousands place it is worth 1000 times d. In the hundreds place it is worth 100 times d.
We are told the difference between those two values is 5400. So 1000 d, minus 100 d, equals 5400.
1000 lots of d, take away 100 lots of d, leaves 900 lots of d. So 900 d equals 5400.
900 d means 900 times d. What undoes times 900?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 900, we divide by 900, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 900. 5400 divided by 900 is 6.
Let's check. A 6 in the thousands place is worth 6000. A 6 in the hundreds place is worth 600. 6000 minus 600 is 5400. It works.
So when the same digit sits in two places, write each place value using a letter, subtract, and solve. The digit is 6.
This number has two stars, and the same digit hides behind both. Let's find out which digit it is.
The same digit is worth different amounts in different places. So, where are the two stars?

ask.ifNot: Count from the right: 2 is in the ones, then a star in the tens, 8 in the hundreds, and the other star in the thousands.

beats.say: Call the digit d. In the thousands place it is worth 1000 times d. In the tens place it is worth 10 times d.
The question says the difference between those values is 6930. So 1000 d, minus 10 d, equals 6930.
1000 lots of d, take away 10 lots of d, is 990 lots of d.
Now d is being multiplied by 990. How do we get d on its own?

ask.ifNot: 990 d means 990 times d, and divide is what undoes times. So we divide both sides by 990.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 990. 990 times 7 is 6930, so d equals 7.
Check it. A 7 in the thousands place is worth 7000, and a 7 in the tens place is worth 70. 7000 minus 70 is 6930. Just right.
So the repeated digit is 7. The trick was to write both place values with one letter, then solve a small equation.
Two stars again, hiding the same digit. But this time we are not told the digit. We are asked what the difference between its two place values could be.
Start with the places. Where do the two stars sit?

ask.ifNot: From the right: 4 is in the ones, a star in the tens, 8 in the hundreds, and the other star in the thousands.

beats.say: Let's try the easiest digit, 1. Then the two place values are 1000 and 10, and the difference is 990.
If the digit were 2, we would get 2000 minus 20. That is just 2 lots of 990. So the difference is always the digit times 990.
So the right choice must be in the 990 times table. 540 is smaller than 990, so it is out. Have a think: which of the others could it be?
2 times 990 is 1980, so 1880 just misses. 3 times 990 is 2970, and 4 times is 3960, so 3030 is skipped too.
Now try the biggest digit, 9. 9 times 990 is 8910. That is one of our choices!
Check with the digit 9. In the thousands place it is worth 9000, and in the tens place 90. 9000 minus 90 is 8910.
So the difference can be 8910. When you do not know the digit, try 1 first and look for the pattern.
Here is a little number machine: 2 X plus 11. X can be any counting number we like. The question asks what kind of number can never come out.
When a question says any number, try a few small ones. With X as 1 we get 13. With 2 we get 15. With 3 we get 17.
Look at 13, 15 and 17. What do they have in common?

ask.ifNot: Look at the last digits: 3, 5 and 7. None of these numbers can be shared into 2 equal groups. They are all odd. And 15 is 3 times 5, so they are not all prime.

beats.say: Is that just luck? No. 2 times any whole number is always even. That is what even means.
And 11 is odd. An even number plus an odd number is always odd.
So 2 X plus 11 is odd every single time. That means it can never be even.
And the other choices? 13 and 17 are prime, so it can be prime. And every answer we got was a whole number. So those can happen.
So the plan: try a few small numbers, spot the pattern, then ask why the pattern must always hold.
Three bags of oranges. We know three totals, so let me write them down in short.
Look at the first two lines. All three bags hold 27, and the first and second together hold 13. Which bag can we find from that?

ask.ifNot: The 13 covers the first and second bags. Take those away from all 27 oranges, and what is left must be in the third bag.

beats.say: So the third bag holds 27 minus 13, which is 14 oranges.
We can use the same idea again. The second and third bags hold 19, so the first bag holds 27 minus 19. That is 8.
Careful now. The question does not want one bag. What is it asking for?

choices: the first and third bags together
ask.ifNot: Read the last line of the question again. It asks how many oranges in all in the first and the third bags.

beats.say: So we add the first bag and the third bag. 8 plus 14 is 22.
Let's check with the second bag. The first two hold 13, so the second has 13 minus 8, which is 5. And 5 plus 14 is 19, just as the question said.
So when you know the whole and a part, subtract to find the missing part. The answer is 22 oranges.
A pen and a pencil cost 18 rupees together, and the pen costs 10 rupees more than the pencil. Let me write that in short.
So a pen is really a pencil with 10 rupees extra. Let me swap the pen for that. Now we have a pencil, plus 10, plus another pencil, making 18.
Take the extra 10 away, and 8 rupees are left. What does that 8 pay for?

ask.ifNot: Look at the line above. Once the 10 is gone, what is left on that side is a pencil and another pencil. So 8 rupees pays for two pencils.

beats.say: Two pencils cost 8 rupees, so one pencil costs half of that, which is 4 rupees.
Now read the question once more. Is 4 our answer?

ask.ifNot: 4 rupees is the price of one pencil. But the question asks how much we pay for 3 pencils.

beats.say: 3 pencils cost 3 times 4, which is 12 rupees.
Check the story. A pencil is 4, so a pen is 4 plus 10, which is 14. And 4 plus 14 is 18. It fits.
So the plan: take off the extra, share what is left equally, then answer exactly what was asked. 12 rupees.
This equation has two letters, a and b. But we are told that b is 3, so only a is really hidden.
First we deal with the b. When b is 3, what does 2 b become?

ask.ifNot: A number written next to a letter means times. So 2 b is 2 times 3, which is 6.

beats.say: So in goes the 3. Now the equation says 7 a, plus 6, minus 2 a, equals 26.
Look for like terms. 7 a and minus 2 a are both a terms. 7 lots of a, take away 2 lots of a, leaves 5 a.
That looks much friendlier. What is in the way of the 5 a?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 5 a has a plus 6 hanging on to it. That is what we clear first.

beats.say: To undo plus 6 we take 6 from both sides, so the balance stays level. 26 minus 6 is 20, so 5 a equals 20.
5 a means 5 times a, so we divide both sides by 5. 20 divided by 5 is 4. So a equals 4.
Check in the equation we started with. 7 times 4 is 28. 2 times 4 is 8. And 28, plus 6, minus 8, is 26. It works.
So the plan: put in the number you are given, gather the like terms, then solve as usual.
We are told x is 8, and we have four equations. Only one of them stays balanced when x is 8. Let's find it.
What is the quickest way to test an equation?

choices: put 8 in for x on both sides
put 8 in on the left side only
ask.ifNot: Solving all four would take ages. It is quicker to put 8 in place of every x, and see whether the left side and the right side come out the same.

beats.say: Start with A. The left side is 8, plus 5 times 8, which comes to 48. The right side is 3 times 8, plus 18, which is 42. They do not match, so A is out.
Now B. On the left we must take 4 times 8, which is 32, away from 9. That goes below zero. The right side is 22. No match.
Now C. The left side is 5 times 8, plus 7. That is 47. Your turn: what is the right side, 8 x minus 17?

ask.ifNot: 8 x is 8 times 8, which is 64. Then we take away 17, and that leaves 47.

beats.say: 8 times 8 is 64, and 64 minus 17 is 47. Both sides are 47. The balance is level!
Let's make sure about D as well. The left side is 39 and the right side is 37. So close, but close is not equal.
So when x is 8, the true one is 5 x plus 7 equals 8 x minus 17.
To test an equation, put the number in on both sides and compare. Equal sides mean it is true.
We are told that 2 m, plus 1, equals 8. And we are asked for 4 m, plus 5. Notice the question never asks for m itself.
Start with the fact. What is in the way of the 2 m?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 2 m has a plus 1 hanging on to it. We clear that first.

beats.say: To undo plus 1 we take away 1, on both sides. 8 minus 1 is 7. So 2 m equals 7.
We could divide by 2 now to find m. But look at what we need: 4 m. How is 4 m related to 2 m?

ask.ifNot: 4 is 2 times 2. So 4 m is 2 lots of 2 m. We do not even need to find m.

beats.say: So 4 m is double 7, which is 14.
Do not stop there! The question wants 4 m, plus 5. 14 plus 5 is 19.
We can check by finding m after all. 2 m is 7, so m is 7 divided by 2, which is 3.5. And 4 times 3.5, plus 5, gives 19 again.
So before you solve for the letter, look at what is asked. Sometimes you can build it straight from what you already know.
Here is an equation with a bracket on each side. Before we can find d, the brackets have to be opened.
On the left, the 2 outside multiplies everything inside. 2 times 3 d is 6 d, and 2 times 4 is 8.
Now the right side. The 4 multiplies the 5, and it multiplies the minus 2 d. What is 4 times minus 2 d?

ask.ifNot: The minus sign belongs to the 2 d, so it comes along. 4 times 2 d is 8 d, and the minus stays: minus 8 d.

beats.say: So 4 times 5 is 20, and 4 times minus 2 d is minus 8 d. The plus 2 at the end just waits.
Tidy the right side. 20 and 2 are both plain numbers, and together they make 22.
Now there are d terms on both sides, and we want them together. How do we bring the minus 8 d over to the left?

choices: write it on the left as − 8d
ask.ifNot: To undo minus 8 d we add 8 d. And whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. A term never just hops across keeping the same sign.

beats.say: So we add 8 d to both sides. On the right it cancels. On the left, 6 d plus 8 d makes 14 d.
Now clear the plus 8 by taking 8 from both sides. 22 minus 8 is 14. So 14 d equals 14.
Divide both sides by 14. 14 divided by 14 is 1. So d equals 1.
Check both sides with d as 1. The left is 2 times 7, which is 14. The right is 4 times 3, plus 2, which is also 14. Balanced.
The plan for brackets: open them first, tidy each side, gather the letters on one side and the numbers on the other, then divide.
Three letters here: p, q and m. But p and q are both built from m. So really there is only one hidden number, m.
Wherever we see p, we can write m plus 3 instead. Wherever we see q, we write 5 minus m. We use brackets, so each one stays together.
Open the first bracket. 2 times m is 2 m, and 2 times 3 is 6.
Now the second bracket. The 3 multiplies the 5, and it multiplies the minus m. What is 3 times minus m?

ask.ifNot: The minus sign belongs to the m, so it travels with it. 3 times minus m is minus 3 m.

beats.say: So 3 times 5 is 15, and 3 times minus m is minus 3 m.
Gather the like terms. 6 and 15 make 21. And 2 m take away 3 m leaves us one m short: that is minus m.
21 minus m equals 0. What must m be?

ask.ifNot: 21 take away something leaves nothing. So that something must be 21 itself.

beats.say: Let's show it the balance way too. Add m to both sides. On the left the m cancels and 21 is left. On the right, 0 plus m is m.
Check. p is 21 plus 3, which is 24. q is 5 minus 21, which is minus 16. 2 times 24 is 48, and 3 times minus 16 is minus 48. Together they make 0.
When letters are built from another letter, swap them in with brackets, open the brackets, and solve as usual.
Look at this. 6 x, plus 9, plus 8 x, minus 5. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's see which.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 6 x is 6 boxes, and 8 x is 8 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 6 x and 8 x together make 14 x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 9 minus 5, which is 4.
So we have 14 x and 4. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 14 x means 14 lots of a hidden number. 4 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 14 x plus 4. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 6 plus 9 plus 8 minus 5, which is 18. The short one is 14 plus 4, also 18. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 5 and y is 1. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 5?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 5.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 5, and 1 y becomes 1 times 1.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 1.
Now add them. 25 plus 1 is 26. So 5 x plus 1 y is worth 26.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
This one is a recipe. Start with 8, multiply it by 2, then add 9. We just have to follow it in the right order.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 2 comes before add 9. So first we work out 8 times 2.

beats.say: So we multiply. 8 times 2 makes 16.
Next the recipe says add 9. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 16.

beats.say: 16 plus 9 is 25. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 2 n plus 9. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 8 in for n. 2 times 8, plus 9, is 25. The same answer. Just never add the 2 and the 9 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 6. We want the value of 3 x, plus 13, minus 5.
Before we swap anything: when x is 6, what is 3 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 3 x means 3 times x, and here that is 3 times 6.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 6 in its place, with a times sign. 3 times 6, plus 13, minus 5.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 3 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 6 is 18. So now we have 18, plus 13, minus 5.
Now we go left to right. 18 plus 13 is 31. Then 31 minus 5 is 26.
That gives 26. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
6 x, plus 6, plus 5 x, plus 8. That is quite a mouthful. Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 6 x is 6 boxes, and 5 x is 5 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 6 x and 5 x together make 11 x.
Now the plain numbers. 6 plus 8 makes 14.
So we have 11 x and 14. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 11 x means 11 lots of a hidden number. 14 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 11 x plus 14. Same value, far fewer pieces.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 36. The short one, 11 times 2 plus 14, comes to 36 as well. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 8 and y is 5. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 2 y.
Before we swap anything: when x is 8, what is 5 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 8.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 8, and 2 y becomes 2 times 5.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 8 is 40. And 2 times 5 is 10.
Now add them. 40 plus 10 is 50. So 5 x plus 2 y is worth 50.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
A number game! Our number is 9. We multiply it by 3, and then we add 11. Let's take it one step at a time.
What do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 3 comes before add 11. So first we work out 9 times 3.

beats.say: 9 times 3 is 27.
Next the recipe says add 11. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 27.

beats.say: 27 plus 11 is 38. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 3 n plus 11. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 9 in for n. 3 times 9, plus 11, is 38. The same answer. Just never add the 3 and the 11 first, because that changes the recipe.
The plan for any number recipe: do the first step, keep the result, then do the next step to that result.
This time the hidden number is not hidden at all: x is 6. So we can work out what 8 x, plus 12, minus 6 is worth.
First, what does 8 x turn into when x is 6?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 8 x means 8 times x, and here that is 8 times 6.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 6 in its place, with a times sign. 8 times 6, plus 12, minus 6.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 8 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 8 times 6 is 48. So now we have 48, plus 12, minus 6.
Now we go left to right. 48 plus 12 is 60. Then 60 minus 6 is 54.
That gives 54. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
Here is a long expression. 2 x, plus 10, plus 7 x, plus 10. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family, and the plain numbers are another. Which two are like terms?

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter part. 2 x and 7 x both have an x, so they are family. 10 has no x at all.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 2 x and 7 x together make 9 x.
Now the plain numbers. 10 plus 10 makes 20.
So we have 9 x and 20. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 9 x means 9 lots of a hidden number. 20 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 9 x plus 20. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 38. The short one, 9 times 2 plus 20, comes to 38 as well. They match.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart.
Two letters this time. x is 4 and y is 2. Our job is to find the value of 2 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 2 x turn into when x is 4?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 2 x means 2 times x, and here that is 2 times 4.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 2 x becomes 2 times 4, and 1 y becomes 1 times 2.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 2.
Now add them. 8 plus 2 is 10. So 2 x plus 1 y is worth 10.
The plan: put the numbers in place of the letters, multiply, then add. A number next to a letter always means times.
A number game! Our number is 6. We multiply it by 3, and then we add 9. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 3 comes before add 9. So first we work out 6 times 3.

beats.say: So we multiply. 6 times 3 makes 18.
Next the recipe says add 9. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 18.

beats.say: 18 plus 9 is 27. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 3 n plus 9. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 6 in for n. 3 times 6, plus 9, is 27. The same answer. Just never add the 3 and the 9 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 2. We want the value of 8 x, plus 2, minus 2.
First, what does 8 x turn into when x is 2?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 8 x means 8 times x, and here that is 8 times 2.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 2 in its place, with a times sign. 8 times 2, plus 2, minus 2.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 8 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16. So now we have 16, plus 2, minus 2.
Look closely: plus 2, and then minus 2. Those two undo each other. So we are left with 16.
That gives 16. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
Look at this. 7 x, plus 7, plus 2 x, plus 9. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's see which.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family, and the plain numbers are another. Which two are like terms?

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter part. 7 x and 2 x both have an x, so they are family. 7 has no x at all.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 7 x and 2 x together make 9 x.
Now the plain numbers. 7 plus 9 makes 16.
So we have 9 x and 16. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 9 x means 9 lots of a hidden number. 16 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 9 x plus 16. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 34. The short one, 9 times 2 plus 16, comes to 34 as well. They match.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart.
Two letters this time. x is 4 and y is 5. Our job is to find the value of 3 x plus 2 y.
Before we swap anything: when x is 4, what is 3 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 3 x means 3 times x, and here that is 3 times 4.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 3 x becomes 3 times 4, and 2 y becomes 2 times 5.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12. And 2 times 5 is 10.
Now add them. 12 plus 10 is 22. So 3 x plus 2 y is worth 22.
The plan: put the numbers in place of the letters, multiply, then add. A number next to a letter always means times.
This one is a recipe. Start with 14, multiply it by 4, then add 5. We just have to follow it in the right order.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 4 comes before add 5. So first we work out 14 times 4.

beats.say: So we multiply. 14 times 4 makes 56.
Next the recipe says add 5. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 56.

beats.say: 56 plus 5 is 61. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 4 n plus 5. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 14 in for n. 4 times 14, plus 5, is 61. The same answer. Just never add the 4 and the 5 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
This time the hidden number is not hidden at all: x is 10. So we can work out what 4 x, plus 12, minus 3 is worth.
First, what does 4 x turn into when x is 10?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 10.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 10 in its place, with a times sign. 4 times 10, plus 12, minus 3.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 4 times 10 comes first.

beats.say: 4 times 10 is 40. So now we have 40, plus 12, minus 3.
Now we go left to right. 40 plus 12 is 52. Then 52 minus 3 is 49.
So when x is 10, the whole thing is worth 49. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.
Here is a long expression. 7 x, plus 8, plus 4 x, plus 10. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter part. 7 x and 4 x both have an x, so they are family. 8 has no x at all.

Look at this one. 5 x, plus 17, equals 97. We want x standing all on its own, so we can see what it is worth.

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 5 x has a plus 17 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: We clear it by doing the opposite: we take away 17. But if we only did that on the left, the balance would tip. So 17 comes off both sides.
On the left the plus 17 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 97 minus 17 is 80. So 5 x equals 80.
Now only the 5 is stuck to the x. 5 x means 5 lots of x. How do we find just one x?

Good mathematicians always check. Put 16 back in place of x. 5 times 16 is 80, and 80 plus 17 is 97. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
